description: How markets bring buyers and sellers together to allocate resources, and the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors.
content_html:
What Is a Market?

When you buy a bus pass, your school orders exercise books, or a landlord rents out a flat, each of those transactions takes place in a market. A market does not have to be a physical place — it is simply any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers together. The stock market operates entirely online. The market for second-hand cars takes place on forecourts, websites and car-boot sales at the same time.

What all markets share is a process of exchange: one party offers something, another party is willing to pay for it, and together they settle on a price. This price sends a signal to everyone else in the market. When the price of petrol rises sharply, drivers cut unnecessary journeys and manufacturers look for cheaper fuel alternatives. The price does not just measure the exchange — it co-ordinates the behaviour of millions of people without any single person directing them.

Key Fact

A market is any opportunity for buyers and sellers to interact in order to establish a price. Markets can be physical (a street market), virtual (eBay) or abstract (the foreign-exchange market).

How Markets Allocate Scarce Resources

Resources are scarce — there are never enough land, labour, capital and enterprise to produce everything everyone wants. Someone must decide what gets produced, how it is produced, and who receives it. In a market economy, those decisions are made through the price mechanism rather than by a central planner.

Think about how this works in the housing market. Demand for homes in city centres is very high; supply is limited. Prices rise. High prices signal to builders that there are profits to be made, so they invest in new construction. Over time — though it can take years — more homes are built and prices moderate. Conversely, if fewer people want to live in a particular town, house prices fall, sending a signal that resources are better used elsewhere. The price mechanism performs three functions simultaneously: it rations the good (only buyers willing to pay the price get it), it signals where resources are needed, and it incentivises producers to respond.

Markets can be divided into two broad types. A factor market is where the inputs to production are traded. The labour market is the most familiar example: firms demand workers and households supply their time and skills, with wages settling at the price where supply meets demand. The market for commercial property is a factor market too — businesses rent factory space and offices.

A product market is where finished goods and services are sold to consumers. The market for smartphones, the market for cinema tickets and the market for takeaway food are all product markets. In a product market, households are the buyers and firms are the sellers — the reverse of a factor market, where firms buy and households sell.

The Three Economic Sectors

Economists divide economic activity into three sectors based on what stage of production is involved. Understanding which sector a business operates in helps us analyse how an economy has changed over time.

The primary sector involves extracting raw materials from the natural environment. A farmer growing wheat, a fishing crew landing a catch, a coal miner cutting seams underground and a forester felling timber are all working in the primary sector. The output is unprocessed — it comes directly from land, sea or underground.

The secondary sector takes those raw materials and turns them into something else. A bakery turning wheat into bread, a car plant turning steel into vehicles, and a construction company building houses are all in the secondary sector. The key activity is manufacturing or processing — adding value to a raw input.

The tertiary sector provides services. A supermarket selling that bread, a bank offering a mortgage, a teacher delivering a lesson, a delivery driver bringing a parcel, a nurse treating a patient — all are in the tertiary sector. No physical good is produced; the value lies in the service itself.

Key Fact

The three sectors are: primary (extract raw materials — e.g. farming, fishing, mining), secondary (manufacture goods — e.g. car production, construction) and tertiary (provide services — e.g. retail, banking, healthcare). In the modern UK, the tertiary sector is by far the largest.

How the Sectors Have Changed in the UK

The relative size of each sector in the UK has shifted dramatically over the past century. In the nineteenth century, the UK was the “workshop of the world”: a huge secondary sector dominated the economy, employing millions in steel mills, shipyards and textile factories. Today that picture looks entirely different.

The primary sector now accounts for a very small share of UK output and employment. Mechanisation of farming, the closure of deep coal mines and the decline of fishing have all reduced the numbers working in primary activities. The secondary sector has also shrunk significantly — a process economists call deindustrialisation. Factories have closed or moved abroad where labour costs are lower, and the UK has shifted away from mass manufacturing.

The tertiary sector now generates the vast majority of UK GDP and employment. Financial services, retail, hospitality, education and healthcare are among the largest employers. Cities like London are global centres for banking and insurance — activities that did not even exist in their modern form a century ago.

Several factors explain why UK manufacturing has declined relative to the service sector. First, global competition: firms in countries with lower wages — such as those in parts of Asia — can produce many manufactured goods more cheaply than UK firms. Second, automation: robots and computer-controlled machinery have replaced manual workers on production lines, so the same level of output requires fewer employees. Third, rising incomes: as people become wealthier, they tend to spend a higher proportion of their income on services — holidays, restaurants, streaming, healthcare — rather than extra manufactured goods. This shifts demand towards the tertiary sector.

Deindustrialisation is not inherently bad: the UK has gained highly productive, high-wage service jobs in finance, technology and the creative industries. However, the transition has been painful for many communities, particularly in the Midlands, South Wales, the North East and parts of Scotland, where manufacturing was the main employer. Structural unemployment rose sharply in those areas when factories closed, because workers’ skills did not immediately transfer to the new service jobs.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to define a market or an economic sector, give a precise, single-sentence answer — a common mistake is being too vague (“a place where things are bought and sold” misses the resource-allocation function and will not earn full marks). For explain questions about the sectors or deindustrialisation, build a chain of reasoning: name the sector or factor, explain the mechanism, then state the consequence. For analyse questions about how markets allocate resources, link the price mechanism’s three functions (rationing, signalling, incentivising) to a named real-world market, and show cause and effect at each step.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A market is any arrangement that allows buyers and sellers to interact to set a price; factor markets trade inputs (such as labour) while product markets trade finished goods and services.
  • The price mechanism allocates scarce resources by rationing, signalling and incentivising — rising prices attract producers; falling prices redirect resources elsewhere.
  • The UK economy is divided into primary (extraction), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services) sectors; deindustrialisation has shifted the UK towards a predominantly service-based economy.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a tertiary sector business?
A) A coal mine
B) A car manufacturing plant
C) A high-street bank
D) A wheat farm
practice_questions.marks: C) A high-street bank [1 mark]. Banks provide a financial service rather than a physical good, placing them in the tertiary sector.

practice_questions.text:
A small furniture company buys timber and turns it into chairs and tables. It employs 12 workers and sells to retail shops.

In which economic sector does this company operate? Show your working.

The company’s annual output is 2,400 chairs. It sells each chair for £85. Calculate the company’s total revenue from chair sales.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the secondary sector (the firm takes a raw material — timber — and manufactures it into a finished good). 1 mark for correct calculation: Total revenue = Price × Quantity = £85 × 2,400 = £204,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain why rising house prices can attract more builders into the housing market.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that rising house prices increase the potential profit for builders; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (higher prices signal that demand exceeds supply, creating an incentive for builders to invest in new construction); 1 mark for linking to the consequence (more homes are built over time, increasing the supply of housing).

practice_questions.text:
A town in the north of England had a large steelworks that employed 3,000 people. The steelworks closed when cheaper steel became available from overseas producers.

Explain how the closure of the steelworks is an example of deindustrialisation, and analyse the likely effects on the local labour market.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining or recognising deindustrialisation (the long-run decline of the secondary/manufacturing sector); 1 mark for applying it to the scenario (the closure of the steelworks reduces secondary sector employment in the town); 1 mark for identifying an effect on the labour market (structural unemployment rises as 3,000 workers lose their jobs); 1 mark for developing the effect (workers’ skills may not match local service sector vacancies, so unemployment may persist even if new service jobs are created nearby).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the price mechanism allocates resources in a market economy, using a real-world market to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A sustained chain of reasoning that identifies and links all three functions of the price mechanism (rationing, signalling, incentivising) with a clearly named market. The response traces how a price change triggers responses from both producers and consumers, leading to a reallocation of resources. Conclusions are specific and well-evidenced.

Secure (3–4 marks): Clear explanation of at least two functions of the price mechanism with a relevant market example. The chain of reasoning is mostly connected but may not fully develop the incentive effect or the reallocation outcome.

Developing (1–2 marks): Some understanding of how prices relate to buyers and sellers, but explanation is underdeveloped. May identify a function without explaining it, or use an example without connecting it to resource allocation.

Emerging (0 marks): No creditworthy economic content.

practice_questions.text:
"The shift from a manufacturing economy to a service economy has been entirely beneficial for the UK."

Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (the shift has been beneficial):
- The tertiary sector now generates the majority of UK GDP, contributing to economic growth and higher average living standards.
- High-skill, high-wage service jobs in finance, technology and the creative industries have replaced lower-paid manual manufacturing roles for many workers.
- The UK’s global competitiveness in financial services and professional services has generated significant export earnings.
- Consumers benefit from a wider range of services, lower prices on manufactured goods (imported cheaply from abroad) and greater choice.

Arguments against (the shift has not been entirely beneficial):
- Deindustrialisation caused severe structural unemployment in former industrial communities, particularly in the Midlands, South Wales and the North East.
- The transition took decades; workers whose skills were built around manufacturing could not quickly retrain for service roles, leading to long-term regional deprivation.
- The UK’s dependence on financial services creates vulnerability: a crisis in the banking sector (as in 2008) can devastate GDP and employment far more than a manufacturing downturn would.
- Not all service jobs are highly paid; many are part-time, low-wage and insecure, so the average figures conceal significant inequality.

Judgement: The answer depends on who is considered and over what time period. For highly educated workers in cities, the transition has been clearly positive. For former mining and steel communities, the costs have been severe and long-lasting. A fully rounded evaluation recognises that the aggregate data can mask deep regional and distributional inequality.

Mastering (8–9 marks): Balanced analysis of both sides with developed, connected chains of reasoning. Judgement is specific and supported (references time period, region, type of worker, or the size of the service sector’s dominance). No significant omissions.

Secure (5–7 marks): Clear arguments on both sides with some development. Judgement present but may be brief or not fully justified.

Developing (2–4 marks): Some relevant points made but argument is one-sided or underdeveloped. Judgement missing or generic.

Emerging (0–1 marks): Limited or no relevant economic content.

options: A market where finished goods are sold to consumers
A market where inputs to production such as labour and land are traded
A market that only operates in physical locations
A market controlled by the government

flashcard_questions.q: What is a market in economics?
flashcard_questions.a: Any arrangement allowing buyers and sellers to interact and establish a price.

flashcard_questions.q: What three functions does the price mechanism perform in allocating resources?
flashcard_questions.a: The price mechanism rations the good among buyers, signals where resources are most needed, and incentivises producers to respond to those signals.
A market where inputs to production — land, labour, capital, enterprise — are traded.
A market where finished goods and services are sold to consumers.

flashcard_questions.q: In a factor market, who are the buyers and who are the sellers?
flashcard_questions.a: Firms are the buyers; households sell their labour and other resources.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the primary sector do?
flashcard_questions.a: Extracts or harvests raw materials directly from the natural environment.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one UK example of a primary sector activity.
flashcard_questions.a: Farming (wheat growing), fishing, or coal mining.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the secondary sector do?
flashcard_questions.a: Takes raw materials and manufactures or processes them into finished goods.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the tertiary sector do?
flashcard_questions.a: It provides services rather than physical goods — the sector includes retail, banking, healthcare, education and transport.
The long-run decline of manufacturing, shifting output and employment towards services.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one cause of deindustrialisation in the UK.
flashcard_questions.a: Competition from lower-wage countries making UK manufacturing less competitive.

flashcard_questions.q: In the modern UK, which sector generates the largest share of GDP?
Why can deindustrialisation cause structural unemployment?
flashcard_questions.a: Workers' manufacturing skills do not directly transfer to new service sector vacancies.

glossary_terms.definition: Any arrangement that allows buyers and sellers to interact in order to exchange goods, services or resources and establish a price.
The condition in which the available supply of a resource is insufficient to meet all the wants of those who desire it.
A system in which resources are allocated primarily through the interaction of buyers and sellers setting prices, rather than by government direction.
A market in which factors of production — land, labour, capital and enterprise — are bought and sold.
A market in which finished goods and services are bought and sold by consumers.
The part of the economy that extracts or harvests natural resources directly from the earth, including farming, fishing, forestry and mining.
The part of the economy that takes raw materials and turns them into finished or semi-finished goods through manufacturing and construction.
The part of the economy that provides services rather than physical goods, including retail, banking, transport, education and healthcare.
The long-run decline of a country's manufacturing and industrial sector, resulting in a fall in the share of employment and output from secondary activities.
